overview: Bunyoro’s history joins political institutions with a regional economy and living Banyoro traditions in western Uganda. Archaeology at Kibiro reveals a long history behind an important salt-producing community, while naming practices express social relationships beyond the kingdom’s borders.

items.text: Excavations at Kibiro on Lake Albert suggest that this important part of Bunyoro’s later economy had origins early in the second millennium CE. That does not date the kingdom’s foundation.
Kibiro’s pottery includes decoration made with carved roulettes. Connah interprets its patterns as evidence of northern connections; this is not a secure ethnic identification.
Empaako names, shared among Banyoro and neighboring communities, express affection, respect and social connection when addressing another person.
A clan head and relatives participate in assigning an Empaako name to a child. UNESCO’s 2013 documentation describes a living practice needing support for transmission.
British conquest caused loss of life and territory. Historians also examine disease and earlier political decisions rather than explaining Bunyoro’s contraction through a single battle.

sources.title: Graham Connah, The salt of Bunyoro: seeking the origins of an African Kingdom (1991)
